items.paragraph: Protecting an old quarter of a city by freezing its buildings in their present form seems the obvious way to preserve its character. It came from the mix of uses, the workshops below flats, the small shops and cheap rooms that let all kinds of people live and work there. Strict rules that forbid any alteration can make buildings expensive to adapt and maintain, so that the craftsmen and small traders move out and the quarter fills with boutique hotels and souvenir shops behind perfectly preserved fronts. Conservation that protects the shell while losing the life it once housed has preserved less than it appears.

items.paragraph: Term limits for legislators are usually defended as a cure for entrenched power: if no one can hold a seat for decades, the argument goes, politics will be refreshed by newcomers who are closer to ordinary citizens. The newcomers do arrive, but the power does not necessarily disappear; it moves. Lawmakers who must leave after a few years have little time to master budgets, procedure or the details of policy, and they come to rely on those who stay: permanent staff, party organisations and lobbyists who have spent years in the building. A legislature of perpetual beginners can thus be more dependent on unelected insiders than one in which some members have served long enough to challenge them. This is not a decisive case against term limits, which may still be worth their costs, but it undercuts the claim that they simply return power to the people.

items.paragraph: A news photograph is often treated as the most neutral element of a report: the words may spin, but the camera simply records. items.paragraph: Procrastination is usually treated as a failure of time management, and the usual remedies follow from that diagnosis: calendars, lists, deadlines broken into smaller pieces. items.paragraph: It is often assumed that digital records, because they can be copied without loss, are safer than paper ones. A manuscript can burn; a file can be duplicated a thousand times. items.paragraph: Where the language of the classroom differs from the language of the home, a common policy is to plunge young pupils into the former from their first day, in the belief that early and total immersion produces fluency fastest. The belief mistakes the job of the early grades. Those years are spent acquiring literacy, number sense and the habit of inquiry, and every one of these comes harder when the medium of teaching is itself a puzzle. A pupil labouring over the sounds of unfamiliar words has little attention left for their sense. Beginning in the home language and bringing in the school language gradually need not hold back fluency in it; children who read confidently in one language generally find that the skill transfers to another.

options.A: Consent always turns what would otherwise be wrong into something permissible, provided the person agreeing understands the terms and signs them of their own accord.
options.B: Employers who offer dangerous work to desperate people act wrongly, and the state should set minimum safety standards that no contract between them may lower.
options.C: Agreements made by workers facing destitution are not real consent at all, and contracts signed under such pressure ought to be treated by the courts as void and unenforceable.
options.D: Consent's power to permit depends on its conditions: agreement forced by desperation shows a preference over disaster, not fairness, so it counts but cannot justify the terms alone.

items.paragraph: Consent is usually treated as transforming what would otherwise be wrong into something permissible: the surgeon's knife, the borrowed car, the signed contract. But the transforming power of consent depends on the conditions under which it is given. A worker who accepts dangerous conditions because the alternative is destitution has agreed, in a sense, and it would be odd to say his signature means nothing. Yet when one party can set the terms and the other can only take them or starve, the agreement shows mainly that the worker preferred this bargain to disaster, not that the terms were fair. To treat such consent as settling the matter is to let the stronger party borrow the moral authority of a free choice that was barely available. Consent remains important; it simply cannot do all the justifying work on its own.

items.paragraph: Most people feel that they would be obliged to help a stranger in danger in front of them, yet feel no comparable obligation to help a stranger in equal danger on another continent. Some philosophers conclude that this feeling is simply a bias: distance, they argue, cannot by itself make a moral difference, so our duties to the distant are as strong as our duties to the near. The argument is powerful, but it moves too quickly. Distance usually travels with other features that may matter, such as whether one is uniquely placed to help, whether one's help will actually arrive, and whether many others could help equally well. To show that the feeling is mere bias, one must show that it survives when these features are held constant, and that is harder than the argument assumes.

options.C: Teenagers who are read to aloud fall behind in reading on their own, since hearing texts spoken stops them from learning to work through difficult sentences unaided.

items.paragraph: Reading aloud is usually treated as something adults do for small children and stop once the children can read for themselves. That timing assumes that the only purpose of listening to a story is to gain access to words one cannot yet decode. But a teenager who reads fluently still gains from hearing a skilled reader. Spoken aloud, a difficult text arrives with its phrasing, pauses and emphasis already worked out, so that sentences which would stall a silent reader become easy to follow, and the listener meets books a little beyond what they would attempt alone. Reading aloud to older pupils is therefore not a step backwards. It serves a different purpose from the bedtime story, and that purpose does not expire once decoding is mastered.

items.paragraph: The placebo effect is often mentioned with a shrug, as if to say that a patient who improves after a sugar pill was never really ill, or only imagined getting better. (3) It would be equally mistaken, however, to treat a dummy pill as a remedy like any other, since relief that rests on expectation may fade once the expectation is withdrawn. (4)
